spec.cue: Hold the phone at the height of a flower and turn slowly. An insect sees nearly all the way around at once, in a coarse mosaic with ultraviolet in it.

fov.note: measured in ants and reported as about 300 degrees; one figure stands for every insect, though a locust reaches 360

cpd.note: a butterfly and an ant resolve about half a cycle per degree; one figure stands for every insect, though locusts and dragonflies are sharper and fruit flies coarser

pupil.note: no record describes a pupil in an insect compound eye

M.note: an ultraviolet, a blue and a green pigment, the classes found in many insects

uvBlue.note: how much of the blue a phone records is read as ultraviolet is a guess

rate.note: 60 divided by about 200 flicker per second, as measured in skippers and nymphalid butterflies; slower insects such as locusts are not covered

insect_uvbg.note: peaks near 360, 440 and 540 nm taken from a copper butterfly and a skipper

field.name: squeeze
field.note: a wide field squeezed toward the middle of the picture

rows: Ants are credited with a visual field of about 300 degrees, and a desert locust's two eyes together cover 360. A fruit fly has a blind patch behind about 50 degrees wide. You very likely see nearly all the way around you.
A Heliconius butterfly resolves about 0.49 cycles per degree and a weaver ant about 0.52, where a human reads about 30. You very likely see the world in a mosaic far coarser than a human's.
A locust at its best resolves about 3 cycles per degree. Dragonflies reach about 2, the finest known among insects, and a fruit fly manages about 0.09.

A copper butterfly has four pigments, peaking near 360, 437, 500 and 568 nanometers. A skipper has two, near 440 and 540, and a cockroach has only an ultraviolet one and a green one. You very likely have an ultraviolet receptor, a blue one and a green one.
A monarch butterfly, a Heliconius butterfly and a fire ant each have a cell most sensitive near 610 to 620 nanometers. A red admiral butterfly has none. You may or may not have this red cell.

A skipper butterfly's eye follows flicker up to about 180 to 200 times a second, a housefly's about 230, and dragonflies go past 300. A locust follows only 30 to 40. You very likely see flicker that a human, who stops at about 60, cannot.
A cockroach's compound eyes still steer its walking by moving stripes at 0.005 lux, about the light of a moonless night.

Nobody has measured how much ultraviolet reaches you from bluish and bright surfaces, and no record describes a pupil in your eyes. One set of numbers stands for every insect, though acuity differs by more than ten times from a fruit fly to a locust.

claims.how: Three records give a visual field of about 300 degrees for ants, and the parameter equals that figure.
0.5 lies between 0.49 cycles per degree in Heliconius erato cyrbia and 0.52 in Oecophylla smaragdina.
The matrix is built from peaks 360, 440 and 540 nm, each equal to a peak stated in these records.
Pigment peaks 360 nm (Lycaena rubidus), 440 nm and 540 nm (Epargyreus clarus) are each stated in a cited record.
Flicker fusion of about 200 Hz lies in 180 to 200 Hz (skipper) and 184 to 204 Hz (nymphalids); 60 / 200 = 0.3.
